analysis.one_liner: Makes drugmakers prove each listed patent covers a distinct invention or lose protection once the first expires.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced January 31, 2025, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, drew no cosponsors, and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a drug-industry practice called patent thicketing. When a drugmaker lists many patents covering one drug, it can sue generic or biosimilar competitors over each patent, delaying cheaper versions for years. The bill would shift the burden: the brand-name company would have to prove in court that each additional patent covers a genuinely different invention, or lose patent protection once the first patent expires. It would also order the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to review whether it is improperly granting multiple overlapping patents on the same drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay brand-name drug prices, and generic and biosimilar manufacturers who want to enter markets sooner. If overlapping patents were cleared away, cheaper copies of drugs could reach the market earlier, lowering prices for consumers, insurers, and government programs like Medicare.

how_it_helps.text: In patent challenges and infringement suits against generic or biosimilar applicants, the patent owner must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that each listed patent covers a patentably distinct invention; otherwise the patents are treated as disclaimed after the first one expires.

The bill directs the USPTO to comprehensively review its examination procedures to reduce the improper issuance of patents that improperly extend a drug's exclusivity, and to report findings and recommendations to the House Judiciary Committee within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose strategies of listing many patents on a single drug to block or delay generic and biosimilar competition would carry a real risk of failing in court. Consumers would bear nothing directly.

drawbacks.text: Stronger generic competition can lower the expected returns on developing improved versions of existing drugs, an argument the industry makes against measures that weaken patent protection.

The bill is narrow: it changes the rules only in specific kinds of proceedings — FDA-related patent challenges under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act, and infringement suits under section 271(e)(2) — and asks USPTO only to study and recommend, not immediately change, its examination practices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is potentially earlier access to cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of drugs whose patents are largely variations on the same invention. The main cost falls on drug companies' profits, not on patients directly. The bill's design has limits: it relies on litigation to enforce the new burden and only studies, rather than directly reforms, the patent office's granting practices, so its real-world effect would depend on how courts apply it. Still, its costs and benefits both point in a clear direction: lower drug prices at the expense of brand-name industry revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors and no hearing, markup, or floor action since it was referred there in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Ryan introduced the bill in the House on January 31, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote has been scheduled or taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off for now: their existing ability to list many patents on a single drug and litigate against generic challengers remains unchanged, and the bill faces long odds with no cosponsors and no committee movement.

for.name: Rep. Patrick Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since it was referred on January 31, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the sole sponsor is a Democrat with no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support is unknown.

industries.note: The bill targets the practice of listing multiple overlapping patents on one drug and suing generic challengers on each one, which can extend a company's monopoly years beyond the first patent's expiry. The industry's interest in keeping that practice runs directly against patients' interest in lower drug prices.

Cheaper generic and biosimilar makers would face fewer overlapping patent suits and could enter markets sooner. Their gain comes from the same outcome patients want: earlier, lower-priced versions of drugs.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, a Republican-controlled House committee holding it, and no action since referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. It would need a committee hearing and markup before any floor vote — a path single-sponsor patent bills rarely complete.
